article.title: Protein across the day: useful habit or another rule to worry about?
article.summary: An even spread of protein can make meals more useful, but short-term synthesis studies do not establish a compulsory eating timetable. Compare the evidence before buying another shake.
article.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
article.intro: Breakfast can be tea and toast, lunch a hurried meal, and dinner the place where nearly all the day's protein finally appears. It is reasonable to ask whether moving some of that protein earlier would help. It is less reasonable to turn that question into a rule that every meal must hit an exact number or the day is wasted. Protein-distribution research is a useful lesson in how an attractive biological idea becomes a stronger claim than the human trials support. The practical opportunity is better meals; the evidence does not require a life organised around a shaker.

sections.title: First check whether there is enough protein to distribute
sections.body: Meal timing cannot compensate for consistently insufficient food. The resistance-training literature addresses the amount available across a day as well as the extra protein supplied by a supplement. Morton's trial synthesis found additional average gains from supplementation during resistance training, with diminishing returns as total intake rose. It does not establish a mandatory amount for every individual or show that a powder is necessary. Before adjusting the clock, write down a few ordinary days of eating, including portions and snacks. A small breakfast may reveal an actual gap, or dinner may simply look large because the other meals contain less obvious sources. An estimate of daily intake provides a better starting point than the number of tubs in a stack.

sections.title: The study that made an even spread appealing
sections.body: Mamerow and colleagues compared evenly distributed and dinner-heavy protein in eight healthy adults. The diets supplied similar energy and protein, which matters: the comparison tested distribution rather than simply adding more food. Over the short feeding periods, the even pattern produced a higher measured rate of muscle protein synthesis across the day. That finding supports a plausible mechanism for making earlier meals more substantial. It does not show that participants became stronger, gained more muscle, or maintained independence with ageing. A tracer can show how quickly new protein is being assembled during a measurement window. The result still needs to survive the much messier test of months of ordinary eating, exercise and recovery.

sections.title: A longer trial did not reproduce a clear advantage
sections.body: Kim and colleagues assigned fourteen older adults to an even or dinner-heavy pattern for eight weeks while keeping daily protein similar. They found no significant between-group differences in lean mass, strength, function or the measured anabolic responses. This was a small study, so it cannot prove that distribution never matters. It does challenge the claim that an even spread reliably produces a large benefit whenever total intake is adequate. The two experiments also differed in age, duration and measurement conditions; they are not exact replications. Reading them together leads to a more useful conclusion than choosing a favourite result: distribution is a reasonable strategy to investigate, while a precise compulsory meal schedule remains a stronger claim than these trials can establish.

sections.title: Ageing changes the question, but does not erase uncertainty
sections.body: In later life, maintaining muscle is about physical function as well as appearance. The practical constraints can include appetite, chewing, cooking, illness and the ability to exercise. A second older-adult trial using integrated measurements over several days found similar muscle protein synthesis with even and skewed patterns when daily protein was sufficient. That is valuable context for claims that older people must follow a rigid distribution formula. It also leaves open questions about people who eat very little, have frailty, or recover from illness: a study in healthy volunteers cannot settle those situations. Making food easier to obtain and eat may be more consequential than enforcing perfect percentages at breakfast, lunch and dinner.

sections.title: Improve the weakest meal without creating a new diet problem
sections.body: An easy application is to inspect the meal that contributes least useful food. For one person, that could mean adding curd to breakfast; for another, eggs, tofu, dal or a suitable milk or soy option may fit better. These are examples of food choices, not interchangeable fixed protein portions: recipes and serving sizes vary. The goal is a meal someone can afford, tolerate and repeat. It need not be numerically identical to dinner. If an extra shake displaces a proper meal, adds unwanted expense, or makes eating more difficult, the distribution project has lost its purpose. A sustainable improvement in the day's food is more useful than an elegant spreadsheet that cannot survive a working week.

sections.title: A powder can fill a gap; its absorption speed is not the whole decision
sections.body: Whey and casein produce different patterns of amino-acid appearance and protein turnover after ingestion. That does not rank every fast product above every slower food for an entire day. A breakfast eaten before a long commute presents a different problem from a meal after training, and both sit inside the overall diet. A powder may be convenient when storage, appetite or preparation time limits food choices. Compare actual labelled protein, allergens, tolerability and cost before paying for a timing claim. The relevant question is whether the product helps solve the identified gap. A premium absorption story has little practical value when an ordinary food or simpler powder already solves it reliably.

sections.title: Judge the habit by outcomes beyond a single anabolic window
sections.body: A study of the response to a very large protein feeding illustrates why one measurement window cannot be treated as the body's universal limit: the investigators observed a prolonged anabolic response after exercise. This does not establish that everyone should eat one enormous meal. It shows that research questions about dose, duration and tissue response need to stay connected to the actual experiment. For an ordinary reader, useful feedback includes whether meals are easier to maintain, training progresses, and appetite and digestion remain manageable. Strength and body-composition changes take time and are affected by training and energy intake. Missing an idealised breakfast is not evidence that the day's protein was wasted.

sections.title: Use distribution as an option, with medical needs taking priority
sections.body: A balanced earlier meal is a sensible option for someone whose current routine makes adequate intake difficult. It is not a diagnosis, and a distribution article cannot set an individual target for pregnancy, illness, frailty or kidney disease. Chronic kidney disease can require an individual protein plan, which changes the meaning of simply adding more. Food allergies and dietary restrictions also determine which sources are appropriate. When comparing products, keep the underlying goal visible: fill a demonstrated dietary gap in a way that fits the person. The evidence supports paying attention to the whole day and the training context; it gives much less reason to pay for anxiety about a perfectly timed scoop.

evidenceNotes.finding: An even distribution increased measured daily muscle protein synthesis in a short controlled experiment.
evidenceNotes.design: Crossover controlled feeding study with tracer measurements.
evidenceNotes.population: Eight healthy adults, mean age about 37 years.
evidenceNotes.outcome: Muscle protein synthesis over short feeding periods.
evidenceNotes.limits: No long-term muscle-size, strength or disability outcome; very small sample.

evidenceNotes.finding: An eight-week older-adult trial found no significant advantage of the even pattern.
evidenceNotes.population: Fourteen older adults with similar total protein in both groups.
evidenceNotes.outcome: Lean mass, strength, function and protein kinetics.
evidenceNotes.limits: Small groups and limited duration leave smaller effects uncertain; healthy volunteers do not represent frailty.
